prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of spherical-aberration correction in electron microscopy, bringing routine sub-angstrom imaging of matter

statement.case_for: Aberration correction is a clear 'invention' in the sense the statutes allow: a long-standing physical limit (Scherzer's theorem, which left round electron lenses with unavoidable spherical aberration) was overcome by multipole correctors designed by Rose, built and made to work by Haider and colleagues, and put to demanding use on real materials by Urban's group. The consequence is measurable and was visible across the whole field within a few years: atomic columns, oxygen positions, vacancies and interface structure in oxides, defects, nanoparticles and 2D materials are now imaged and analysed quantitatively, with spectroscopic mapping at the same resolution. Two decades of commercial use and thousands of independent instruments mean there is no doubt about maturity or reproducibility. I read the discovery-or-invention criterion as satisfied here at least as cleanly as for most candidates on the list. I should also be candid that no colleague ranked B011, so this is a case I have to argue rather than one the opening ballots support. Having read the others, my judgement is that B052 is the strongest consensus candidate and I would not regard it as a poor prize; but B011 is the one I would defend as the most original and least replaceable contribution, and I do not think breadth of opening support should substitute for scientific merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is framing and attribution. First, some colleagues may regard an instrumentation advance as enabling methodology rather than a discovery in physics; I disagree, but the committee must be able to state in the citation what it is physics-wise (a solution to a fundamental limit in charged-particle optics with new access to atomic-scale structure). Second, credit is genuinely split across two lineages, the TEM corrector (Rose, Haider, Urban) and the STEM corrector (Krivanek, Dellby and colleagues), and the three credited names cannot cover both. A citation for 'aberration correction in electron microscopy' risks being read as overlooking the STEM line, so the wording would have to be tied carefully to what the three named people did, and I rely on my own knowledge of that history, not on verified sources. Third, I am the only member to rank this first, and my experience as a TEM user may inflate how obvious the importance appears to others.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B052) are a clean two-person configuration (Katori, Ye) and the kind of measurement-limited advance he values most, with 1e-18 uncertainties and independent confirmation across laboratories.
responses.response: I agree on the merit and ranked B052 third myself, so I am not contesting that it would be a deserving prize. But the criterion he applies, a measurement-limited advance with broad downstream use, is exactly what aberration correction offers in a different domain, and it cuts at least as sharply in favour of B011. I would also stress the overlap he himself raises with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize: it should be addressed in the citation rather than dismissed, and the pending redefinition of the second is a timing argument that applies to B052 and not to an instrument already in use for twenty years. I would support B052 as a fallback; I do not accept that it is clearly the stronger scientific case.

responses.point: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B021) form a coherent theory-plus-experiment trio (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), mature, with decades of independent confirmation, though the credited set omits other contributors.
responses.response: I ranked B021 second and agree on the field's importance. My reservations are the ones he partly raises: the experimental credit rests on HgTe, not on graphene, where the Kane-Mele gap is too small to observe, so the citation cannot honestly say the effect was demonstrated in the system that was proposed. I would add the priority problem around the HgTe proposal (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and the 3D generalization, and a thematic closeness to the 2016 topological-phases prize. Those are the reasons I place it as an alternative rather than first. I would welcome his view on how the committee should word a citation that is fair to the 2D and 3D parts without a four- or five-person list.

responses.point: The experimental Higgs discovery (B010) is the unrecognised half of a closed story, with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as founding leaders of ATLAS and CMS, and he accepts the configuration is defensible but imperfect.
responses.response: I take the point that the discovery is overdue in a scientific sense, but I disagree that leadership credit solves the attribution problem. The three named people conceived and built the detectors, which is a different contribution from the 2012 analyses, and the prize would then reward detector leadership for a result obtained by thousands. I raise this because I have the same difficulty with my own candidate's credit and with B043 (which I ranked fourth): in each case the committee must say what the named individuals actually did. For B011 that is simple, since the corrector is an object that three people designed and made work. For B010 it is not, and I think that weakens the case relative to what the opening ballots suggest.

responses.point: For B021 he notes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing from the credited names, which weakens fairness, and that the topology theme was recognised in 2016.
responses.response: I agree with both points, and they are why I do not make B021 my preferred prize despite ranking it second. I would go slightly further: the omission is not just a matter of fairness, since the HgTe observation by Molenkamp was motivated by that proposal, so the experimental half of the citation depends on credit the list cannot give. Where I differ is on weight: he ranks it eighth, but I think the overlap with 2016 (which honoured topological phase transitions and phases in a different context, 1D and 2D integer quantum Hall systems) is arguable and is not by itself disqualifying.

responses.point: WMAP (B006) turned CMB anisotropy into a precision Lambda-CDM parameter set, very mature and arguably overdue, while acknowledging that COBE (2006) and the 2019 cosmology prize complicate the credit boundary.
responses.response: I can judge the physics only as an informed outsider, so I will defer on the cosmology. My concern is the one he states: after COBE and Planck, the committee needs a precise argument for why the WMAP increment is a separate discovery rather than a refinement. If that argument is made persuasively I would view B006 as a serious contender, but at the moment I do not see it yet in the opening statements.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues accept aberration correction as a discovery-or-invention achievement in physics, since no one else ranked B011.

Whether the citation can be framed so that it is fair to the STEM corrector lineage (Krivanek, Dellby) despite a three-name list limited to Rose, Haider and Urban; this rests on my recollection of the history and not on supplied evidence.
How to weigh the broader opening support for B052 against my own judgement about originality and replaceability.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 overlaps weaken B052 enough to change the ordering.
Whether a two-part configuration is realistic: B052 (two people) plus any part of B011 would exceed the three-person limit unless the B011 credit were split, which I would not support.
statement.conflict_note: As a transmission electron microscopist at Chalmers I work directly with the technique in B011, and I am the only member to have ranked it first. The provided profile documents no personal, collaborative or institutional connection to Rose, Haider or Urban, so no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile, but the field proximity could be seen as a bias and the committee may wish to note it. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, though his top candidate (B056) is not in my preferred configuration.
